misreading.wrong: Christianity fell silent after 1989 because secular hostility silenced it: the problem is the modern world's refusal to listen to the Church's message.
misreading.right: Ratzinger blames believers: having privatized God and lived etsi Deus non daretur, faith arrived in public with a God who had nothing to do.

argument.tension: After 1989 the world hungered for an alternative, yet Christianity, long privatized, could not speak into the public arena.
argument.move: He indicts not secularism but believers' practical atheism, then asks what faith must bring with it out of the ghetto.
argument.payoff: Faith re-enters public life carrying its distinctive feature: God as judge, limit, standard, origin and goal of history.

rubric: Blames believers' privatized God, not secularism
Names etsi Deus non daretur as the drift
Public faith brings God as judge and goal

misreading.wrong: Faith and unbelief are opposites: the believer is secure, the unbeliever has settled the question and lives at peace without God.
misreading.right: Both live in doubt: the believer is threatened by unbelief, the unbeliever by the “perhaps” that belief may after all be true.
misreading.quote: It is not until belief is rejected that its unrejectability becomes evident.

argument.tension: The believer faces the plunge into nothingness; the unbeliever faces the possibility that belief may still be the truth.
argument.move: He rejects the clown analogy: both sides share doubt and belief, so doubt becomes their avenue of communication.
argument.payoff: Neither side can close itself off; the terrible “perhaps” keeps both honest and open to each other.

rubric: Doubt threatens both believer and unbeliever
The “perhaps it is true” cannot be escaped
Doubt enables communication between both sides

misreading.wrong: Believing means accepting unproven claims about the invisible, a private leap of feeling that reason cannot touch and need not justify.
misreading.right: Credo is a fundamental mode of behavior toward reality: conversion to the conviction that the unseen is the truly real sustaining everything.
misreading.quote: Belief has always had something of an adventurous break or leap about it

argument.tension: Man's eyes grasp only the visible, yet his existence cannot live on the visible alone; God never enters that field.
argument.move: He defines credo as conversion: a second access to reality that judges the visible by the unseen true reality.
argument.payoff: Faith becomes a daily about-turn, undemonstrable yet reasonable: a basic decision no human can avoid making.

rubric: Credo is conversion, not inference
The unseen is the truly real
Undemonstrable because only the turned receive it

misreading.wrong: The obstacle to belief is outdated language: modernize the Gospel's wrapping and the message becomes credible again for today.
misreading.right: The real scandal is God's self-commitment to history: the eternal became one man we can kill, and no reinterpretation may dissolve this offense.
misreading.quote: God has come so near to us that we can kill him

argument.tension: Belief seems mere loyalty to yesterday, yet beneath that lies Christianity's positivism: God committed to one figure, one hour.
argument.move: He exposes the deeper offense behind the old-fashionedness, then calls inoffensive reinterpretations dishonest before the non-Christian's “perhaps not”.
argument.payoff: Honesty is restored: the Gospel may offend, but it stands on reality instead of dissolving into viable propositions.

rubric: Distinguishes secondary then-now scandal from positivism
Revelation makes God touchable and killable
Inoffensive interpretation betrays honesty

misreading.wrong: Because truth is what we make, theology should present faith as history or as world-changing praxis to remain rational and relevant.
misreading.right: Vico's factum and Marx's faciendum reduce truth to the made and makable; belief lives on neither plane but in stand-understand.
misreading.quote: all that we can truly know is what we have made ourselves

argument.tension: The modern mind admits as real only the made and the makable, while faith concerns what was never made by us.
argument.move: He traces truth's reduction from being to factum to faciendum, then finds belief's place not in know-make but stand-understand.
argument.payoff: Faith escapes both rescue attempts: it is entrusting oneself to meaning that no making could produce.

rubric: Explains verum quia factum then faciendum
Belief is not know-make but stand-understand
Faith entrusts to meaning not made

misreading.wrong: Faith is the opposite of reason: it believes where proof ends, so understanding must wait until knowledge catches up.
misreading.right: Faith is standing firm on received ground; understanding grows from that standing, so believing and understanding are inseparable, not rivals.
misreading.quote: Meaning that is self-made is in the last analysis no meaning.

argument.tension: Practical knowledge can make everything except meaning, yet man cannot live without meaning; making cannot ground itself.
argument.move: From Isaiah's 'mn root he draws faith as entrusting oneself, taking a stand; only from standing does understanding grow.
argument.payoff: Becomes clear that meaning is received not made; entrusting oneself to the unmade ground enables all human making.

rubric: Faith is taking a stand on received ground
Meaning is received, never self-manufactured
Believing and understanding are inseparable

misreading.wrong: The “Amen” of faith is a blind leap beyond reason: mystery excuses contradictions, and faith thrives where argument fails.
misreading.right: Amen is a movement toward logos and truth; it is practical knowledge that renounces truth, and mystery serves understanding, never failed reason.
misreading.quote: Truth is the only ground suitable for man to stand upon.

argument.tension: Calculating knowledge succeeds by asking only what functions; faith insists on what things are in truth and meaning.
argument.move: He reverses the cliché: faith seeks logos and truth, while practical knowledge renounces truth; mystery grounds understanding instead of excusing failure.
argument.payoff: Meaning, ground and truth stay indivisible; theology becomes a rational task and faith escapes fideism.

rubric: Amen is movement toward logos, not surrender
Calculating knowledge renounces truth itself
Mystery grounds understanding, never excuses absurdity

misreading.wrong: Believing in you is private sentiment: personal trust in Jesus replaces argument, so faith needs no reflection once the heart is moved.
misreading.right: Christian faith's center is a “you”: in Jesus the world's meaning is a person who loves me, and love keeps asking “Are you really he?”
misreading.quote: its central formula is not “I believe in something”, but “I believe in you.”

argument.tension: Faith in a spiritual ground of the world remains “something”; Christian faith finds the world's meaning as a person addressing me.
argument.move: He passes from the logos that upholds all things to the encounter with Jesus, where meaning becomes love that loves me.
argument.payoff: Believing, trusting, loving unite; every thesis of the Creed expresses this one about-turn, yet love keeps the question alive.

rubric: Faith's object is a “you”, not something
In Jesus meaning is present as love
Love itself demands asking “Are you he?”

misreading.wrong: The twelve apostles each contributed an article to the Creed, so its authority rests on their personal authorship.
misreading.right: The Creed grew from Rome's three-question baptismal dialogue; the apostolic-authorship story is a later legend, yet it faithfully echoes the ancient Church's faith.
misreading.quote: the oldest form of the confession of faith takes the shape of a tripartite dialogue

argument.tension: The text bears all the marks of history — legend, regional rivalry, imperial politics — yet carries the ancient Church's faith.
argument.move: He narrates the Creed's real growth from baptism, then shows West's salvation-history and East's cosmic emphasis as complementary accents.
argument.payoff: Historical messiness becomes no obstacle: at decisive points the Creed is an accurate echo of the New Testament message.

rubric: Creed arose from baptismal question and answer
Apostolic article-authorship is later legend
East-West differences are emphasis, not contradiction

misreading.wrong: The Creed's entanglement with politics and division is an embarrassment to be explained away before its teaching can be trusted.
misreading.right: The muddle is instruction: faith's great leap happens on the petty human scale, so faith must involve forgiving and needing forgiveness.
misreading.quote: faith has to do, and must have to do, with forgiving

argument.tension: The Creed unites all believers, yet its history shows division, regional interests and imperial manipulation woven into its very text.
argument.move: Instead of excusing the tangle he reads it: the leap occurs amid all-too-human circumstances, exposing man as a divided being.
argument.payoff: Believing is shown as inseparable from forgiving; man finds himself only in receiving and transmitting forgiveness.

rubric: Faith's leap occurs on the petty scale
The muddle reveals man's divided greatness
Faith necessarily entails forgiving

misreading.wrong: Dogma is a fixed list of doctrines to be recited and obeyed; its authority lies in the precision of its propositions.
misreading.right: Dogma serves the conversion enacted in baptism: “I believe” means “I hand myself over to” — the whole person's turn to the invisible.
misreading.quote: The phrase “I believe” could here be literally translated by “I hand myself over to”, “I assent to”.

argument.tension: Dogma looks like recited doctrine, yet its birthplace is baptism's renunciation-and-assent, a shift of the whole being.
argument.move: He returns to the original dialogue form — question, renunciation, assent — showing councils sought right doctrine as right conversion.
argument.payoff: Dogma is relocated as the form of a conversion — about-turn of existence — not a fossilized catalogue of theories.

rubric: Faith is conversion, renunciation and assent
“I believe” means “I hand myself over”
Dogma serves the about-turn, not recitation

misreading.wrong: The Creed is the Church's substitute for personal faith: real believing is one's own private search for truth.
misreading.right: Faith comes from hearing, not private reflection; as symbolon each believer holds only a broken half, completed only with others.
misreading.quote: Christian belief is not an idea but life

argument.tension: Philosophy thinks alone and then speaks; faith is spoken to from outside and must answer within a “We”.
argument.move: He unfolds “symbolon”: each holds a broken half, so word, common confession and Church belong to faith's own nature.
argument.payoff: Community and creed are not additions: Christianity is truth as a way, mind incarnate in the body of history.

rubric: Faith comes from hearing, not private thought
Symbolon: each believer holds only half
Church and confession belong to faith itself
